chapter_theme: Twenty four-gem verses on what ruins and what sustains (disunity, bad company, enmity, the giving hand), the stages of learning, kinds of joy and refuge, and a birth-ranking set against verses that deny birth any hold on fortune.

21.reading: Disunity ruins strength, falsehood ruins a man's gold-like body, the vessel it is poured into spoils the taste of milk, and joining with those one should not join ruins a lineage.
21.nuance: Each gem has the same verb, சிதைக்கும், so the verse is a list of what ruins what; the milk spoiled by its vessel is the image that explains the last gem, bad company spoiling a family. ஒருவனை on line 1 can go with the disunity (it ruins a man's strength) or with the falsehood of line 2; the reading takes the second.

items.claim: lack of unity ruins strength
falsehood ruins a man's gold-like body
the vessel milk is poured into spoils its taste
joining with those one should not join ruins one's lineage

22.reading: Unfailing clarity is what brings renown, folly is what makes one overstep and act without regard for others, bewilderment is what makes one a blind man who sees nothing, and learning is what gives eyes cleared of darkness.
22.nuance: கற்பு here is learning, not chastity: it is set against மம்மர், the blindness of bewilderment, and gives eyes free of darkness. The four make two pairs, a gain against a fault and a blindness against a sight.

items.claim: unfailing clarity brings renown
folly makes one transgress and neglect others
bewilderment makes one a blind man who cannot see
learning gives eyes from which darkness has gone

23.reading: The elephant bears its load even when it struggles, the child that is beaten still runs to its mother crying 'mother', friends even when angry do nothing that makes one tremble, and there is no time when the hostile live together with one.
23.nuance: Three bonds hold under strain (each with பினும், 'even if') and the fourth, the enemy, never binds at all. மலைப்பினும் வாரணம் தாங்கும் is taken as the elephant bearing its rider though it rages; it may mean a protector who stands firm though attacked.

items.claim: the elephant still bears its burden even when it struggles
the child, though beaten, runs to its mother crying 'mother'
friends, though angered, do nothing that makes one tremble
the hostile never have a time of dwelling together with one

24.reading: The good of laughter grows among friends, the good of a fine assembly shines through good will, the good of a swift chariot is won through its driver, and the good of a town is weighed by the one who dwells in it.
24.nuance: Each நலம் depends on someone other than the thing itself: friends, kindness, a driver, an inhabitant. உள்ளான் may be the town's leading man rather than any resident.

items.claim: the good of laughter flourishes among friends
the good of an assembly shines through love
the worth of a swift chariot gains distinction through its driver
the good of a town is judged by the one within it

25.reading: The verse, in the second person, names four things: if one fears anything, to fear fearlessness; not to fall short of what befits one, to the full of one's means; not to swerve from what the heart knows even for a crore of wealth; and not to pry into a task left with friends.
25.nuance: Each of the first three plays a negative noun against its own verb (அஞ்சாமை அஞ்சுதி, எஞ்சாமை எஞ்சல், கோடாமை கோடி); the second is the hardest to construe and may mean not leaving undone what one can do.

items.claim: fearlessness is the thing to fear, if one fears at all
not falling short of what suits one is to be kept to the full
not swerving against one's conscience holds even for a crore
a task entrusted to friends is not to be scrutinised

26.reading: Rearing other living beings to torment them is a fault, buying flesh at a price and eating it is a fault, saying what should not be said is a fault, and killing is a fault too.
26.nuance: The buyer's eating and the killer's act are counted as two separate faults, and a fault of speech sits between them; அலைப்பான் may mean rearing beings for slaughter rather than for torment.

items.claim: rearing other beings in order to torment them is a fault
buying flesh at a price and eating it is a fault
saying what should not be said is a fault
killing too is a fault

27.reading: All the people live looking to the sceptre, infants live looking to their mother's breast milk, the world lives looking to the rain from the sky, and Death rejoices looking to the world's dying.
27.nuance: Three dependencies on a giver are closed by a fourth that inverts them: Death too 'lives looking', but to the world's end, and is glad of it.

items.claim: all the people live by looking to the king's sceptre
infants live by looking to the mother's milk
the world lives by looking to rain from the sky
Death rejoices looking to the world's dying

28.reading: As one learns, deep ignorance lessens; as it lessens, freed of meanness, one grasps the nature of this world; grasping it, one walks the path of truth; and that path sets fame in this world and enters the high world beyond.
28.nuance: The four gems are links of one chain, each clause's result the next clause's condition, so learning leads by stages to the other world. The verse runs to five lines where the rest have four.

items.claim: learning lessens deep ignorance
when ignorance lessens one is freed of meanness and grasps the world's nature
grasping that nature, one walks the path of truth
that path sets fame here and enters the higher world

29.reading: Water stays where there is a hollow, sin stays where many cast blame, desire stays where it crowds in destroying, and understanding stays where something befalls oneself.
29.nuance: Each thing is placed by where it 'stands' (நிற்பது, -உழி), so the last makes understanding something that shows itself in one's own trouble. அழித்துச் செறிவுழி is hard; it may mean where desire, having broken restraint, presses close.

items.claim: water settles where there is a hollow
sin stays where many cast blame
desire stays where it presses in, destroying
understanding stands firm where trouble befalls oneself

30.reading: Nothing is mightier than fortune, nothing suits a man better than learning, of all things nothing is more painful than poverty, and nothing is firmer than the strong hand that never says 'there is none'.
30.nuance: Four superlatives: the pain of want (line 3) is answered by the giving hand (line 4). வன்பாட்டது, read as 'firmer', may instead mean harder in labour.

items.claim: nothing is mightier than fortune
nothing suits a man better than learning
nothing is more painful than poverty
nothing is firmer than the hand that never says 'there is none'

31.reading: Blazing fire appears with smoke as its seed, joy appears with laughter as its seed, enmity sprouts with a man's own former intent as its seed, and once sprouted it becomes the seed of suffering.
31.nuance: The seed image runs through all four, and the last turns the third forward: enmity is both a sprout of one's own intent and the seed of further pain. முன்னம் may also mean a prior deed.

items.claim: blazing fire appears from smoke as seed
joy appears from fine laughter as seed
enmity sprouts from a man's prior intent as seed
once sprouted, enmity becomes the seed of suffering

32.reading: Women who do not look ahead are like a disease, loving people are like an ornament to the world, men of mean understanding are like weeds in a crop, and the hard-hearted are like stone.
32.nuance: The only item that names a sex judges women, and பின்நோக்கா ('not looking behind') is unclear: heedless of consequence, or not looking after the household. The other three are men or people at large.

items.claim: women who do not look ahead are like a disease
loving people are like an ornament to the world
men of mean understanding are like weeds among crops
the hard-hearted are like stone

norm.note: a judgment of the period on women's conduct, likening heedless women to disease

33.reading: There is no birth better than the brahmin's, whatever one does; no kin more excellent than the mother; no beauty equal to prosperity; and nothing to compare with youth.
33.nuance: அந்தணர் here ranks a birth-group above all others, a caste ranking stated as fact. என்செயினும் ('whatever one does') can close line 1, making the brahmin's birth best whatever he does, or open line 2, making the mother the best kin whatever she does; the caste claim is much stronger on the first reading.

items.claim: no birth is better than the brahmin's
no kin is more excellent than the mother
no beauty equals prosperity
nothing compares with youth

norm.note: a birth-rank of the period: the brahmin's birth ranked above all others

34.reading: Iron is split by iron, those who have drunk water rinse the mouth with water, rare things are won, on examination, by rare means, and great things are reached through great men.
34.nuance: Two physical cases of like working on like (iron on iron, water on water) prove the two moral ones; the mouth-rinsing is cited as a familiar act, not laid down as a rule.

items.claim: iron is split by iron
those who drink water cleanse their mouths with water
rare things are obtained by rare means
great things are reached through the great

35.reading: The frenzy of valour shows before kings, the joy of virtue shows when one gives to those who have nothing, the joy of conceit falls upon the poor, and the joy of the base blares through the town.
35.nuance: Four kinds of களி (elation) are told apart by where they show. வியக்களி நல்கூர்ந்தார் மேற்றாம் may mean a poor man's empty pride or the boast of the rich made over the poor.

items.claim: the elation of valour shows before kings
the elation of virtue shows in giving to those who lack
the elation of conceit falls upon the poor
the elation of the base is trumpeted through the town

36.reading: Flower-like eyes brighten with collyrium, an upright flame in the dark night grows with ghee, the kuruku leaf sprouts when rain pours and thunder roars, and friends flourish the more when one gives.
36.nuance: The verb தளிர்க்கும் ('puts out shoots') makes all four things grow from what they are fed. Whether the friends flourish when one gives to them, or one flourishes when friends give, the line allows both; குருகிலை is an uncertain plant name.

items.claim: flower-like eyes brighten with collyrium
an upright flame grows with ghee in the night
the kuruku leaf sprouts with pouring, thundering rain
friends flourish the more when there is giving

37.reading: Laughter is sweet among friends, a store of wealth is sweet if one gives it out with one's own hand, a woman of good kind is sweet if she tends and serves, and music is sweet in the hearts of those who understand song.
37.nuance: Each sweet thing is sweet only under a condition (among friends, if given, if she serves, to the knowing), so the verse ranks the condition above the thing. The woman's sweetness is made to depend on her service.

items.claim: laughter is sweet in the midst of friends
a store of wealth is sweet if given out by one's own hand
a woman of good kind is sweet if she tends and serves
music is sweet in the hearts of those who understand song

norm.note: a period norm making a woman's worth depend on her tending and service

38.reading: For those who hide what they have, the end they come to is always downfall; for those who beg, the refuge is those who give; for a wide army, the support is valour; and for living beings, the refuge is others' not eating flesh.
38.nuance: செல்சார் ('the place one goes to') is a refuge in three items and an ironic destination in the first: the hoarder's only refuge is ruin. The last item gives the creatures' side of abstaining from flesh.

items.claim: downfall is the end that comes to those who hide their wealth
givers are the refuge of those who beg
valour is the support of a wide army
not eating flesh is the refuge of living beings

39.reading: Craftsmen make what they have seen, the learned do what they have heard to be so, those close to one do the sweet things one desires, and fortune does what the unresentful intend.
39.nuance: The first three are sources of action (sight, hearing, another's wish); the fourth gives fortune itself to the patient. புலனாள்வார் is read as the learned, and அமைந்தார் as intimates; both words allow other senses.

items.claim: craftsmen make what they have seen
the learned do what they have heard to be so
those close to one do the pleasing things one wants
fortune does what the unresentful intend

40.reading: Fortune does not abide by rank of birth, mighty Death does not take its food by doing what it is told, desire does not stay hidden however hard one hides it, and justice stands as the king is.
40.nuance: Three things no human order controls are set beside a fourth that depends wholly on one man, the king. திணைவகையான் may mean by class of birth or by kind of person.

items.claim: fortune does not stay according to rank or kind
Death does not act at anyone's bidding
desire cannot be hidden however hard it is hidden
justice stands according to the king

links.note: Naladiyar 177 says water mixed with milk becomes milk, so the small are hidden by joining the great; Nanmanikkadigai says the vessel spoils the milk, as bad company ruins a lineage.
links.teaches: The same mixing image runs both ways in the group, the good absorbing the small in one and the container corrupting the good in the other, so company is shown to work in both directions.
links.list_adds: It sets the spoiled milk among four kinds of ruin (disunity, falsehood, bad company), so mixing is counted as a cause of loss, not of concealment.

links.note: Verse 22 says learning gives eyes cleared of darkness; verse 28 traces learning step by step through lessened ignorance to the path of truth and the higher world.
links.teaches: Read together, the single sight learning gives in 22 becomes in 28 the first link of a chain that ends beyond this world.

links.note: Kural 805 tells one to read a friend's hurtful act as folly or intimacy; Nanmanikkadigai says friends, even angry, do nothing that makes one tremble.
links.teaches: The couplet expects friends to wound and supplies a charitable reading, while the verse sets a limit no anger crosses, so the pair marks how far a friend's hurt may go.
links.list_adds: It ranks the friend with the elephant and the beaten child as bonds that hold under strain, against the enemy who never stays, a contrast the couplet lacks.

links.note: Both verses open with laughter among friends: in 24 its good grows there, in 37 it is sweet there.
links.teaches: The book twice makes friendship the condition of laughter, once as growth and once as pleasure, so laughter is never praised in itself but only in company.

links.note: Kural 428 calls not fearing what should be feared folly; Nanmanikkadigai says that if one fears anything, it should be fearlessness itself.
links.teaches: The couplet sorts objects of fear, while the verse turns fear on the fearless disposition, so the danger moves from the thing feared to the temper of the man.
links.list_adds: It makes the fear of fearlessness the first of four checks on oneself, with not falling short, not swerving for wealth and trusting friends, so fear opens a short code of integrity.

links.note: Kural 510 says doubting one already trusted brings endless trouble; Nanmanikkadigai says not to pry into a task left with friends.
links.teaches: The couplet states the general error of doubting the trusted, and the verse turns it into a working rule about checking up on a delegated task.
links.list_adds: It puts non-interference with friends' work beside refusing a crore against one's conscience, so trust in friends is counted as part of one's own integrity.

links.note: Kural 256 argues that buyers cause the killing, since no one would sell flesh if none bought; Nanmanikkadigai counts buying and eating flesh as a fault in its own right.
links.teaches: The couplet needs an argument to make the buyer guilty, while the verse simply lists buying and killing as two faults, showing the group's code taking the Kural's conclusion as settled.
links.list_adds: It sets the buyer's fault beside the killer's and beside rearing beings to torment them and improper speech, so flesh-buying becomes one of four plain faults rather than the end of an argument.

links.note: Both lists put killing and eating flesh beside a fault of speech: Nanmanikkadigai saying what should not be said, Sirupanchamoolam speaking evil of a girl without inquiry.
links.teaches: Two counted works independently join a speech fault to the code of non-killing, so harmful words are filed with harm to bodies across the group.

links.note: Kural 542 says the world looks to the sky and the people to the sceptre; Nanmanikkadigai keeps both and adds the infant at the breast and Death looking to the world's end.
links.teaches: The verse borrows the couplet's two dependencies and closes them with Death's grim watch, so the image of living by looking to a giver ends in the one watcher who takes.
links.list_adds: It adds the infant's dependence on milk and inverts the series with Death, so the king's sceptre is one giver among nurturers set against a taker.

links.note: Kural 398 says learning gained in one birth protects through seven; Nanmanikkadigai traces how learning reaches the other world step by step.
links.teaches: The couplet states that learning outlasts a life, and the verse supplies the stages by which it does so, ignorance lessening into insight, insight into the true path, the path into fame and the higher world.
links.list_adds: It turns the couplet's single benefit into a chain of four causes, so the reward beyond this life is earned through intermediate changes in the learner.

links.note: Kural 421 calls understanding the tool that guards against ruin; Nanmanikkadigai says understanding is found standing where trouble befalls oneself.
links.teaches: The couplet gives understanding its use as a guard, and the verse gives the place where it is proved, one's own adversity.
links.list_adds: It sets understanding among things known by where they settle (water in a hollow, sin under blame, desire in a crowding), so understanding is defined by its location in trouble.

links.note: Kural 1041 says nothing is more painful than poverty except poverty itself; Nanmanikkadigai names poverty the most painful of all things.
links.teaches: The couplet leaves poverty incomparable, while the verse places the hand that never refuses right after it, so the extreme of want is paired with the extreme of giving.
links.list_adds: It makes the pain of poverty one of four superlatives and follows it with the generous hand, so the list supplies the remedy the couplet leaves out.

links.note: Kural 871 says enmity should not be wanted even in jest; Nanmanikkadigai says enmity sprouts from a man's own prior intent and then becomes a seed of suffering.
links.teaches: The couplet warns against wanting enmity, and the verse explains why: it grows from one's own intention and multiplies into more pain.
links.list_adds: It sets enmity beside fire from smoke and joy from laughter, so laughter seeds joy while intent seeds enmity, a contrast to the couplet's 'not even in jest'.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai likens the hard-hearted to stone; Naladiyar 334 ranks stones above base people because stones at least serve whoever uses them.
links.teaches: The two verses use stone in opposite ways, as hardness to be blamed and as plain usefulness to be praised, so the base man is lower than the very thing the hard-hearted resemble.
links.list_adds: It makes stone one of four likenesses (disease, ornament, weeds), so the image names a kind of person rather than ranking people against things.

links.note: Reading என்செயினும் with line 1, Nanmanikkadigai holds the brahmin's birth best whatever he does; Kural 134 says a brahmin's birth is ruined when his conduct fails.
links.teaches: On that reading the two make incompatible claims about whether conduct can forfeit a high birth, which shows the group divided on birth against conduct.
links.list_adds: It ranks brahmin birth alongside the mother, prosperity and youth as unequalled goods, so birth is treated as a fixed endowment like youth, not a standing to be kept.

links.note: Nanmanikkadigai ranks the brahmin's birth above all others; the Siddhar verse asks whether a number is marked on flesh or bone to tell a Paraiyar woman from a Brahmin woman.
links.teaches: Set together, a birth-rank stated as plain fact meets a later denial that birth leaves any mark on the body, showing the claim the ethics work takes for granted being contested.

links.note: Verse 33 ranks brahmin birth highest; verse 40 says fortune does not abide by rank or kind.
links.teaches: The book ranks births yet denies that birth secures fortune, so within one work high birth is honoured but given no hold on prosperity.

links.note: Kural 443 calls winning the great as one's own the rarest of rare things; Nanmanikkadigai says great things are reached through great men, as iron splits iron.
links.teaches: The couplet prizes the great as companions, and the verse explains the worth by a law of like working on like, so the great are needed because only they can reach great ends.
links.list_adds: It proves the claim with two physical cases (iron on iron, water rinsing after water), so the moral rule is given the force of a natural one.

links.note: Kural 1076 likens the base to a beaten drum that proclaims secrets; Nanmanikkadigai says the elation of the base blares through the town.
links.teaches: The couplet shows the base unable to keep others' secrets, and the verse shows them unable to keep their own joy quiet, so loudness marks them in both.
links.list_adds: It sets the base man's elation against the warrior's before kings and the giver's before the poor, ranking kinds of joy by where they show.

links.note: Kural 260 says all creatures fold their hands to the one who neither kills nor eats flesh; Nanmanikkadigai says others' not eating flesh is the refuge of living beings.
links.teaches: Both speak from the side of the creatures, the couplet as their worship and the verse as their shelter, so abstaining from flesh is a protection given, not only a purity kept.
links.list_adds: It puts abstention beside givers as the beggar's refuge and valour as an army's, so refusing flesh is counted among the supports others depend on.

links.note: Kural 1253 has a woman say her desire shows like a sneeze though she would hide it; Nanmanikkadigai says desire cannot be hidden however hard one tries.
links.teaches: The lover's confession in the couplet becomes in the verse a general law, so a moment of love poetry is used as ethical knowledge.
links.list_adds: It sets desire beside fortune and Death as things no one controls, so its showing is ranked with impersonal forces rather than one woman's weakness.

source_issues: 28: five lines where the other verses have four.
